(p-177) Surah al-Nahl

Makkī in its entirety according to al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah and Jābir. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is Makkī except for three verses from it, which were revealed in Madīnah, namely His saying ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾ up to His saying ﴿And We will surely reward those who were patient with the best of what they used to do﴾. They were revealed after the killing of Ḥamzah at Uḥud.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾. Concerning it there are three interpretations. The first: it means "the command of Allah will come," in the sense of the future. The second: its meaning is "the command of Allah has drawn near." The third: it is used in its literal sense of "coming," in the sense of its being established and settled.

Concerning ﴿the command﴾ there are four opinions. The first: it is the warning of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), said by Abū Muslim.

(p-178) The second: it is His obligations and rulings, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The third: it is the threat to the people of polytheism and the victory of the Messenger (ﷺ), said by Ibn Jurayj.

The fourth: it is the Resurrection, which is the view of al-Kalbī.

It is reported from Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: when ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ was revealed, they raised their heads, and then ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ was revealed, meaning: do not seek to hasten its occurrence.

Muqātil ibn Sulaymān related that "when Jibrīl recited to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾, the Messenger of Allah rose in fear of its occurrence until he recited ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾." It may bear two meanings. One: do not seek to hasten the denial, for it will not be delayed. The second: do not seek to hasten its coming before its appointed time, for it will not come early.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 2:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾. Regarding this there are five interpretations.

The first: that the Spirit here is the revelation (al-wahy), which is prophethood. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it is the speech of Allah Most High, which is the Qur'an. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The third: that it is the clarification of the truth that must be followed. This was said by Ibn Isa.

The fourth: that it refers to the spirits of creation. Mujahid said: No angel descends except that with him is a spirit.

The fifth: that the Spirit is mercy. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

It may also admit a sixth interpretation: that the Spirit is guidance, because hearts are given life by it just as the spirit gives life to bodies.(p-179)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 3–4:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He created man from a drop of sperm; and behold, he is an open adversary.﴾ Al-khasim (adversary) is one who argues in disputation, and al-mubin (open, manifest) is one who expresses clearly what is in his inner self.

Regarding the description of him by this, there are three aspects. The first: to make known the power of God, may He be exalted, in bringing him out of the lowly drop until he became in this state of eloquence and capability.

The second: to make him know the blessings of God, may He be exalted, upon him in bringing him to this state after having created him from a lowly drop.

The third: to make him know the gravity of what he committed of squandering the blessing by disputing in disbelief. This was said by al-Hasan.

Al-Kalbi mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi when he took decayed bones, crumbled them, and said: "Will we be brought back when we become like this?"

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verses 5–7:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And the cattle — He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat.﴾ ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home at evening and when you send them out to pasture.﴾ ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not reach except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾ Regarding "warmth" (al-difʾ) there are three opinions. The first: it is clothing; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: what you warm yourselves with from their wool, fur and hair; this was said by al-Hasan. The third: that "warmth" refers to their young offspring that are not ridden; this was related by al-Kalbi.

As for ﴿and benefits﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: offspring (al-nasl); this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it means riding and labour.

﴿And from them you eat﴾ means milk and meat.

(p-180) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home at evening and when you send them out to pasture﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: "ruwah" (bringing home) is their return from the pastures to the encampments, and "sarah" (sending out) is their dispersal from the encampments to the pastures. The second: it applies generally to all their states, whether going out or returning, from pasture, work or riding. As for the "beauty" in them, there are two views. The first: the saying of al-Hasan, "When they see them: these are the camels of so-and-so," this was said by al-Suddi. The second: the turning of people's gaze towards them, and this is a possible reading.

He mentioned "ruwah" before "sarah" although the latter comes after it, because their milk is then at its fullest and because the soul is more delighted by it.

﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not reach except with great hardship to yourselves﴾: concerning "the land" there are two views. The first: that it is Makkah, because it is among the lands of deserts (al-falawat). The second: that it is to be understood generally, for every land whose route is by the back (of the animal).

Regarding ﴿except with great hardship to yourselves﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: that without them you would not have reached it except with great hardship to yourselves. The second: that even with riding them you would not reach it except with great hardship to yourselves, so how would it be for you if they did not exist.

Regarding "shiqq al-anfus" (great hardship to yourselves) there are two interpretations. The first: exertion of the self (jahd al-nafs), derived from "al-mashaqqah" (hardship). The second: that "shiqq" means "half", so it is as though it takes away half of the self.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 8:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: what you do not know of creation, and this is the view of the majority (al-jumhur).

The second: it refers to a spring (ʿayn) beneath the Throne, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

(p-181) The third: what has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ), that it is a white land the distance of a thirty days' journey by the sun, filled with creatures who do not know that Allah is disobeyed on earth. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, then where is Iblis among them?" He said: "They do not know that Allah created Iblis." Then he recited: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾.

﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way, and among them is that which deviates﴾ may bear two meanings:

First: Upon Allah is the aiming at truth in judgment among His servants, and among them is one who deviates from truth in his judgment.

Regarding "them" there are two opinions. First: they are the people of the diverse desires (ahl al-ahwa'), as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: the religions of disbelief (milal al-kufr).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 14–18:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And you see the ships ploughing through it﴾ (mawakhir fihi). There are five opinions regarding it. The first: that mawakhir means heavily laden (mawaqir), said by al-Hasan.

The second: that they are the ones that run through it crosswise, said by Abu Salih.

The third: that they cut through the wind from the ships (yamkhuru al-rih), said by Mujahid, because al-makhr (cutting through) in their speech means the blowing of the wind.

The fourth: that they run with one wind, coming and going, said by Qatadah.

The fifth: that they are the ones that split the water from the right and the left, because al-makhr in their speech means splitting the water and stirring it, said by Ibn Isa.

﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾ (wa li-tabtaghu min fadlihi) admits of two meanings. The first: by trade upon it. The second: by what you extract from its ornaments (halyah) and eat of its flesh.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And landmarks; and by the star they are guided﴾ (wa 'alamat wa bil-najm hum yahtadun). Regarding "landmarks" (al-'alamat) there are three opinions. The first: that they are the markers of the road by day, and by the stars they are guided by night, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that they too are the stars, since some stars are used for guidance, said by Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Nakha'i.

The third: that the landmarks are the mountains.

Regarding "the star" (al-najm) there are two opinions:

(p-183) The first: that it is a collective noun for the fixed stars, expressed in the singular to indicate the category.

The second: that it refers specifically to al-Jady (the Pole Star), alone, because it is the most firmly fixed of all the stars in its place.

Regarding the meaning of being guided by it, there are two opinions. The first: that it intends being guided by it on all journeys, said by the majority (al-jumhur).

The second: that it intends being guided by it toward the qiblah.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about His, the Exalted, saying ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾, and he said: 'It is al-Jady, O Ibn 'Abbas; your qiblah is upon it, and by it you are guided on your land and your sea.'"

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ (wa in ta'udda nimata Allahi la tuhsuha). There are two opinions regarding it. The first: "you could not preserve it" (la tahfazuha), said by al-Kalbi.

The second: "you could not thank for it" (la tashkuruha), and this is transmitted from the early authorities (ma'thur).

The intended meaning of this statement admits of two possibilities. The first: that it comes in the manner of bestowing favor, magnifying His blessing such that it cannot be counted.

The second: that it is a magnification of the thanks due to Him, such that it cannot be fully rendered.

According to the first opinion, it comes in the manner of bestowing favor.

According to the second opinion, it comes in the manner of seeking forgiveness (al-ghufran).

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ That is: and when it is said to those previously mentioned, those who do not believe in the Hereafter and whose hearts deny the Resurrection.

﴿in full on the Day of Resurrection﴾ This may have two meanings. One: that it has not been removed by repentance.

The second: that it has not been lightened by afflictions.

﴿and [also] some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾ This means that along with the burdens they have carried, they will also bear the burdens of those whom they led astray.

The second: its meaning is that what they have borne of their burdens distresses them.

According to the first meaning, it is hastened in this world, and according to the other meaning, it is deferred to the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 26–27:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Those before them had already schemed, so Allah came at their structures from the foundations﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first: He demolished their buildings from their foundations, which is the base (asas).

The second: it is a parable (mathal) that Allah, exalted is He, struck for their annihilation.

﴿So the roof fell down upon them from above them﴾. On this there are two aspects. The first: the upper parts of their houses fell down while they were beneath them, and therefore He said ﴿from above them﴾, although we know that a roof is high, yet it would not be "above them" unless they were beneath it. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: meaning that the punishment came to them from the sky, which is above them. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Regarding those upon whom the roof fell from above them, there are three sayings. The first: they were Nimrod ibn Kanaan and his people when he wanted to ascend to the heaven and built the tower (al-sarh). So Allah demolished it upon him. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Zayd ibn Aslam.

The second: they were Bukhtnasar (Nebuchadnezzar) and his companions. This is the view of some of the exegetes.

The third: meaning the Muqtasimun (those who divided the Qur'an), whom Allah mentioned in Surah al-Hijr. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

The first: that Paradise is better than the Fire; and although this is known, what is meant by it is giving them the good news of their deliverance from it. The second: that He intended that the Hereafter is better than the abode of this world; this is the view of most (scholars).

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good﴾ — it was said its meaning is "righteous."

It may also mean "good of soul," confident in what they will meet of God's reward.

And it may admit a third interpretation: that their death is a good, easy death, without hardship or pain, unlike the manner in which the soul of the disbeliever is seized.

The second: that it is good news to them of Paradise, because peace is security.

The second: that they say this to them in the Hereafter.

(p-191) His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not seen what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline about, to the right and to the left, prostrating to Allah, and they are humbled?﴾ Regarding ﴿whose shadows incline about﴾ there are four interpretations:

First: its shadows return, because al-fay' (the shade) means return; for this reason the shade after the zawal (the decline of the sun from its zenith) is called fay', because it returns.

Second: its meaning is that its shadows incline; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: its shadows revolve; this was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Fourth: its shadows shift; this was said by Muqatil.

﴿to the right and to the left﴾: regarding this there are two interpretations. First: it means that at times they incline toward the right and at times toward the left; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, because the shadow follows the sun wherever it turns.

Second: the right is the beginning of the day and the left is the end of the day; this was said by Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

﴿prostrating to Allah﴾: regarding this there are three interpretations. First: the shadow of everything is its prostration; this was said by Qatadah.

Second: the prostration of the shadows is the prostration of their bodies (ashkhas); this was said by al-Dahhak.

Third: the prostration of the shadows is like the prostration of the bodies; they prostrate to Allah in humility; this was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid.

Al-Hasan said: "As for your shadow, it prostrates to Allah, but as for you, you do not prostrate to Allah. By Allah, how evil is what you have done!"

﴿and they are humbled﴾ means they are abased and submissive. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"There remained only one who is humbled in the enclosure, and one who is confined, in other than your land, a confined one."

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creature, and the angels﴾. As for the prostration of what is in the heavens, it is a prostration of submission and worship. As for the prostration of what is on the earth of creatures, it admits two interpretations. First: their prostration is their submission to Allah, exalted is He.

Second: the manifestation of the power of Allah in them obliges the servants to prostrate to Allah, glorified is He.

(p-192) Regarding the singling out of the angels by mention, although they are included among those in the heavens and the earth, there are two interpretations. First: He singled them out by mention because of their distinction in rank, so He distinguished them from the whole by mention, although they are included in it.

Second: because they are excluded from the group of those that crawl (yadibbu), since Allah has given them wings, so they are not included in the group; therefore they were mentioned.

A third answer: on the earth there are angels who record the deeds of the servants, who are not included among the angels of the heaven; therefore He singled them out by mention.

﴿and they are not proud﴾ admits two interpretations. First: they are not proud to prostrate to Allah, exalted is He. Second: they are not proud to submit to the power of Allah.

﴿They fear their Lord from above them﴾: regarding this there are two interpretations. First: it means the punishment of their Lord from above them, because punishment descends from the sky. Second: they fear the power of Allah, which is above their power and is in all directions.

﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾: regarding this there are two interpretations. First: it refers to worship; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Second: it refers to exacting retribution from the disobedient.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verses 56–60:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿When one of them is given the news of a female, his face becomes darkened, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ Regarding His words ﴿darkened﴾ (*musawaddan*, from *aswadda*, "to become black") there are three interpretations. The first: it means black in color, said by the majority of scholars. The second: its color is changed, either to blackness or to something else, said by Muqatil. The third: the Arabs say of anyone who meets with something disagreeable that "his face has blackened" from distress and sorrow, said by al-Zajjaj.

From this comes the expression "I blackened the face of so-and-so," meaning "I caused him distress."

Regarding His words ﴿and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾ (*kazim*) there are three interpretations. The first: *kazim* means one who is grieved, said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it is one who suppresses his anger and does not show it, said by al-Akhfash. The third: it is one who is distressed and clamps his mouth shut so that he does not speak, derived from *al-kizama* (the stopper, i.e., the sealing of the mouth of a waterskin), said by Ibn Isa.

Regarding His words ﴿Shall he keep it in disgrace?﴾ (*'ala hawn*) there are three interpretations. The first: *hawn* is *al-hawan* (disgrace) in the dialect of Quraysh, said by al-Yazidi. The second: *hawn* means "little" in the dialect of Tamim, said by al-Farra'. The third: *hawn* means affliction and hardship, said by al-Kisa'i.

al-Khansa' said:

*We debase our souls, and the lowering of souls*
*on the day of harm is better for them.*

Regarding His words ﴿or bury it in the dust?﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: it refers to the buried infant girl (*al-mawudah*), who is buried alive in the dust by killing her. The second: it refers to concealing her from people so that they do not recognize her, like one buried in the dust, hidden from sight. This second interpretation is possible.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil description﴾ may carry two meanings. The first: the evil attribute of ignorance and disbelief. The second: God described them with the evil attribute concerning companions and offspring.

﴿And to God belongs the highest description﴾ has two meanings. The first: the supreme attribute, that He is the Creator, the Provider, the All-Powerful, and the Recompenser. The second: sincerity and monotheism, said by Qatadah.

The second: that He hastens it in this world.

If it is said: How can He encompass them all with destruction when among them there is a believer who is not a wrongdoer? In response to this there are three answers. The first: He makes the destruction of the wrongdoer a retribution and a recompense, and the destruction of the believer is compensated by the reward of the Hereafter.

The second: ﴿He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾ from among the people of wrongdoing.

The third: meaning that if He destroyed the fathers for their disbelief, the sons would not exist and the offspring would be cut off, so no believer would be born.

The second: its meaning is that for them from Allah is the good recompense; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: its meaning is, certainly, theirs is the Fire.

The third: their deeds necessitated that theirs is the Fire.

The third: removed far away in the Fire; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Abu Ja'far al-Qari' read (mufarritun) with a kasra on the ra' and a shadda, and its meaning is from neglect (tafrit) in what is obligatory.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 70:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions. The first: it means the lowest and most decrepit (awdaʿahu wa-anqasahu), said by the majority (al-Jumhur).

The second: it is the senile old age (al-Haram), said by al-Kalbi.

The third: it is eighty years, related by Qutrub.

The fourth: it is seventy-five years, said by ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿So that he will not know, after knowledge, anything﴾. This means that he returns to being ignorant, not knowing anything, as he was in his childhood.

Or, because he has forgotten what he used to know, and does not acquire what he does not know.

And it may bear a third meaning: that its sense is "so that he will not act, after knowledge, with anything." Here He expressed action by knowledge (al-ʿilm), because of its dependence upon it; for the effect of old age on his action is more pronounced than its effect on his knowledge.

(p-201)

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying: ﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision﴾. Concerning this there are three aspects. The first: that He made some rich and some poor, and expanded and restricted [provision].

The second: concerning contentment (al-qana'ah) and desire (al-raghbah).

The third: concerning knowledge and ignorance.

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: The most excellent provision a person is given is a knowledge that guides him to his Lord, and an intellect that guides him to his right course.

Regarding the favouring there are two aspects. The first: that He favoured masters over slaves; this is what Ibn Qutaybah said, and whoever holds that the favouring is in wealth.

The second: that He favoured free persons over one another; this is what the majority (al-Jumhur) said.

﴿So those who have been favoured do not return their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they are equal therein﴾. Concerning this there are two aspects. The first: that since they do not make their slaves partners in their wealth, it is not permissible for them to make partners with Allah, exalted is He, in His dominion. This is what Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said, and in this is evidence that the slave does not own [property].

The second: that they and their slaves are equal in that Allah, exalted is He, provides for all of them, and that no one is able to provide for his slave unless Allah, exalted is He, grants that provision to him, just as he is not able to provide for himself. This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

﴿Do they then deny the blessing of Allah?﴾ Concerning this there are two aspects. The first: they deny what Allah has bestowed upon them of His bounty and provision. The second: they go astray despite what Allah has bestowed upon them of His proofs and guidance.(p-202)

The Exalted said: ﴿And Allah has made for you spouses from yourselves.﴾ On this there are two views. The first: it means He made for you, from your own kind, counterparts like you, and He coined the image of "from yourselves." This is the view of Ibn Bahr.

The second: it means Adam, from whom He created Hawwa' (Eve). This is the view of most scholars.

﴿And made for you, from your spouses, sons and grandchildren (ḥafadah).﴾ Regarding al-ḥafadah there are five views. The first: they are the in-laws, the sons-in-law of a man through his daughters. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Duha, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibrahim. From this is the poet's verse:

"Had my soul obeyed me, it would have made for her
a ḥafad of many who could be counted.
But it is a soul that is proud toward me,
averse to the in-laws of the base, and disdainful of them."

The second: they are the grandchildren. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: they are the sons of a man's wife by another husband. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: they are the helpers. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The fifth: they are the servants. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatada and Tawus. From this is Jamil's verse:

"The young slave-girls hastened around them,
and they gave up with their hands the reins of the camels."

Tarafa ibn al-'Abd said:

"They hasten to serve the guest in their tents,
out of generosity, and that is from them without humiliation."

The root of ḥafd (حَفْد) is haste, and ḥafadah is the plural of ḥāfid (حافِد), who is one who is quick in work. From this is their saying in the qunut: "And to You we strive and hasten" (وإلَيْكَ نَسْعى ونَحْفِدُ), that is, we hasten to work in obedience to You. From this is al-Ra'i's verse:(p-٢٠٣)

"I burdened, with its unknown destination, eight she-camels
when the drivers hastened upon their saddles."

Some scholars, in interpreting the Exalted's words ﴿sons and ḥafadah﴾, said: the sons (banīn) are the young, and the ḥafadah are the grown-ups.

﴿Then in falsehood do they believe?﴾ On this there are two views. The first: in idols. The second: they deny resurrection and recompense.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 77–79:

(p-205) His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾ may bear five meanings:

First: the knowledge of the unseen of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, because He alone possesses it, to the exclusion of His creation.

Second: the meaning of "the unseen" is the bringing into existence of what does not exist and the annihilation of what exists.

Third: it means the doing of what has been and what will be, whereas what exists at present is known.

Fourth: the unseen of the heavens is the requital with reward and punishment, and the unseen of the earth is the decreeing of provisions and terms of life.

﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as the blink of an eye, or it is nearer﴾. This is because it is equivalent to His saying: ﴿Be, and it is﴾. He named it "the Hour" only because it is a part of the Day of Resurrection, and the parts of a day are its hours.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil mentioned that the unseen of the heavens is the establishment of the Hour.

Muqatil said: the occasion of its revelation was that the disbelievers of Quraysh asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the establishment of the Hour, mocking it, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 80–83:

His, Mighty and Majestic is He, saying: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from what He has created, shades﴾. In this there are two views. The first: they are houses. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: they are trees. This was said by Qatada.

﴿And He has made for you, from the mountains, shelters (akhnan)﴾. Akhnan is the plural of kinn, which is the place in which one takes shelter. In this there are two views:

(p-206) The first: that it is the shade of the mountains.

The second: that it is what is in them of caves or high places.

﴿And He has made for you garments (sarabil) that protect you from the heat﴾. It means garments of cotton, linen and wool.

﴿And garments that protect you from your violence﴾. It means the coats of mail that protect against violence (ba's), which is war.

al-Zajjaj said: Everything that is worn of a shirt or coats of mail is a sirbal (garment).

If it is said: How did He say ﴿And He has made for you, from the mountains, shelters﴾ without mentioning the plains, and said ﴿that protect you from the heat﴾ without mentioning the cold? To this there are three answers. The first: that the people were people of mountains and were not people of plains, and were people of heat and were not people of cold, so He mentioned to them His blessings upon them that are specific to them. This was said by Ata.

The second: that He suffice with mention of one of the two over mention of the other, since it is known that whoever takes shelters from the mountains takes them from the plains, and the garments that protect from heat protect from cold. This was said by al-Farra', and similar to it is the saying of the poet:

؎ And I do not know, when I aim for a land seeking good, which of the two will befall me.

So he alluded to the evil without mentioning it, because it is indicated by what is said.

The third: that He mentioned the mountains because He had mentioned the plains earlier, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a dwelling﴾, and mentioned the heat without the cold as a warning against the heat of Hell and as a guarding against deserving it through refraining from sins.

﴿Thus He completes His blessing upon you, that perhaps you may submit (tuslimun)﴾, meaning that you may believe in Allah when you recognize His blessings upon you.

Ibn Abbas recited la'allakum tusallimun with a fatha on the ta', meaning that you may be safe (taslamun) from harm. It is possible that he meant the harm of heat and cold, and it is possible that he meant the harm of fighting and killing, and it is possible that he meant the harm of punishment in the Hereafter if you take heed and believe.

His, Mighty and Majestic is He, saying: ﴿They recognize the blessing of Allah, then they deny it﴾. In this there are five interpretations:

(p-207) The first: that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ): they recognize his prophethood, then they deny it and call him a liar. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: that they recognize what Allah, Exalted is He, enumerated for them in this surah of blessings, and that they are from Allah, but they deny them by saying that they inherited that from their fathers. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: that their denial is that a man says: Had it not been for so-and-so, such-and-such would not have happened, and had it not been for so-and-so, I would not have obtained such-and-such. This was said by Awn ibn Abdullah.

The fourth: that their recognition of the blessing is their acknowledgment that Allah provided for them, and their denial is their saying: We were provided that through the intercession of our gods.

The fifth: they recognize the blessing of Allah by enjoying it, and they deny it by failing to give thanks for it.

It may also be understood, as a sixth: they recognize it in hardship and deny it in ease.

And it may also be understood, as a seventh: they recognize it with their words and deny it with their deeds.

al-Kalbi said: This surah is called the Surah of Blessings, because of the abundance of Allah's blessings upon His creation that He mentions in it.

﴿And most of them are disbelievers﴾. In this there are two views. The first: its meaning is that all of them are disbelievers, and He expressed the whole by the majority. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Hasan.

The second: He said ﴿and most of them are disbelievers﴾ because among them are those upon whom the ruling of disbelief applies by virtue of others, such as children and the insane, so the mention is directed to those who are legally responsible.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 89:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And on the Day We raise up in every nation a witness against them from among themselves﴾. They are the Prophets, witnesses over their nations on the Day of Resurrection. In every age there is a witness, even if he is not a prophet.

Regarding them there are two opinions. The first: they are the imams of guidance (a'immat al-huda), who are the successors (khulafa') of the Prophets.

The second: they are the scholars (al-'ulama') through whom God preserved the sacred laws (shara'i') of His Prophets.

﴿And We have brought you as a witness over these﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ) as a witness over his community.

(p-209) His words, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾ — to the end of the verse.

There are three opinions regarding the interpretation of this verse.

The first: justice is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and excellence is patience in obeying His command and avoiding His prohibition, and obedience to Allah both in private and in public. ﴿And giving to kinsfolk﴾ is maintaining family ties. ﴿And He forbids immorality﴾, meaning fornication, ﴿and wrongdoing﴾, meaning ugly deeds. ﴿And transgression﴾ is arrogance and injustice; this is related from Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

The second: justice is judging with truth, and excellence is bestowing favor through generosity, and giving to kinsfolk is what they deserve of maintenance (nafaqat). ﴿He forbids immorality﴾ is the ugly deeds that are committed in secret. ﴿Wrongdoing﴾ is what is openly committed and is denounced. ﴿Transgression﴾ is that by which one exalts oneself through injustice and otherwise. This is the meaning of what Ibn 'Isa mentioned.

The third: justice here is the equality of the inner and outer state in acting for Allah. Excellence is that one's inner state be better than one's outward state. Immorality and wrongdoing are that one's outward state be better than one's inner state. This was said by Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna.

Thus He commanded three things and forbade three things.

﴿He admonishes you that you may remember﴾ may have two meanings: first, that you may remember what He has commanded you and what He has forbidden you; second, that you may remember the reward He has prepared for obedience to Him and the punishment for disobedience to Him.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verses 91–92:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And fulfil the covenant of Allah when you have covenanted﴾ admits of three interpretations. The first: it refers to vows (nudhur).

(p-210) The second: what one has pledged to Allah of a covenant in obedience to Allah.

The third: it is the commitment to the rulings of the religion after entering into it.

﴿And do not break oaths after their confirmation﴾ admits of three interpretations. The first: do not break them by refusing after confirming them through commitment. The second: do not break them with an excuse after confirming them through fulfilment. The third: do not break them by violating them (hinth) after confirming them through piety (birr).

There are three opinions regarding this verse. The first: it was revealed concerning the pledge of allegiance (bay'ah) to the Prophet ﷺ. The second: it was revealed concerning the alliance (hilf) that existed in the Jahiliyyah among the people of polytheism, and Islam came to require fulfilling it. The third: it was revealed concerning every oath (yamin) that a person binds himself to voluntarily, the fulfilment of which is obligatory unless a necessity calls for its dissolution.

The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "(Let him come to that which is better)" is to be understood as applying to necessity, not to what is merely permissible.

The people of the Hijaz say: "I confirmed this oath (wakkadtu hadhihi al-yamin) with confirmation (tawkidan)," while the people of Najd say: "I confirmed it (akkadtuha) with confirmation (ta'kidan)."

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And do not be like her who unravels her spun thread after it was strong, into pieces (ankathan)﴾. This is a parable that Allah the Exalted struck for one who breaks his covenant, and concerning it there are two views. The first: that it refers to the rope, and it is expressed by "spun thread," said by Mujahid. The second: that it literally refers to spun thread.

﴿After it was strong﴾ has two views. The first: after being twisted (ibram). Said by Qatadah.

(p-211) The second: the "strength" is what has been spun on a spindle and not yet twisted (lam yuthn).

﴿Into pieces (ankathan)﴾ means unravelled (ankadan), its singular is nakth, and everything that is unravelled after being twisted is ankath.

It was said that the woman who unravelled her spun thread after it was strong was a foolish woman in Mecca. Al-Farra' said: she was Rayta bint 'Amr ibn Ka'b ibn Sa'd ibn Taym ibn Murrah, called Ja'dah because of her foolishness; she used to spin wool and then unravel it after twisting it. So when this act, if you had done it out of folly, you would have denounced, likewise is the breaking of a covenant, which you do not denounce.

﴿Taking your oaths as deceit between you (dakhalan baynakum)﴾ has six interpretations. The first: that dakhal means delusion (ghurur). The second: that dakhal means deception (khada'ah). The third: that it means rancour (ghill) and cheating (ghish). The fourth: that it is what lies within the heart of treachery, contrary to what is outwardly shown of adherence to fulfilment. The fifth: that it is treachery and betrayal, said by Qatadah. The sixth: that it is breaking (hinth) oaths that have been confirmed.

﴿That one community may be more numerous than another (an takuna ummatun hiya arba min ummah)﴾: meaning that it is greater in number and more abundant in support, so that by its multitude it seeks to betray the smaller one by exchanging the covenant of the smaller for the covenant of the greater.

"Arba" is the comparative form (af'al) of riba (excess), the poet said:

"And a dark, spear-like (khatti) lance whose joints are like the stone of a date-pit, or exceeding by a span of ten."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 97:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾. Concerning it there are five interpretations:

First: that it is the lawful provision (al-rizq al-halal). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: that it is contentment (al-qanaʿa). This was said by ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Hasan al-Basri.

Third: that it is that he is a believer in Allah, acting in obedience to Him. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Fourth: that it is happiness (al-saʿada). This is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Fifth: that it is Paradise. This was said by Mujahid and Qatada.

It may also admit a sixth interpretation: that the good life is well-being (al-ʿafiya) and sufficiency (al-kifaya).

It may also admit a seventh interpretation: that it is contentment with the decree (al-ridaʾ bi-l-qadaʾ).

﴿And We will surely reward them with their best deeds, of what they used to do﴾. It admits two meanings. The first: that they are rewarded for the best of their deeds, which is obedience, excluding the permissible (al-mubah) among them. The second: the multiplication of the reward, which is the better of the two, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times the like thereof﴾ [al-Anʿam: 160].

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verses 98–100:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: "When you intend to recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah, the Exalted." This was said by al-Zajjaj.

(p-213) The second: "When you are a reciter, seek refuge in Allah."

The third: that it is of the inverted (al-mu'akhkhar) which means the preposed (al-muqaddam), and its sense is: "When you have sought refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan, then recite the Qur'an."

Al-isti'adhah (seeking refuge) is the seeking of the repelling of harm by the Most High, in a manner of submission and humility. The meaning is: seek refuge in Allah from the whisperings of Satan at the time of your recitation, so that you may be safe in the recitation from slipping, and in the interpretation (ta'wil) from error.

We have mentioned in the opening of the book the meaning of "al-rajim" (the accursed).

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: "He has no power to lead them into a sin that will not be forgiven." This was said by Sufyan.

The second: "He has no proof for what he calls them to of disobedience." This was said by Mujahid.

The third: "He has no authority over them, because of their seeking refuge in Allah from him," due to the words of the Most High: ﴿And if a prompting from Satan should incite you, then seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ [Fussilat: 36].

The fourth: that he has no authority over them in any way, because Allah the Most High turned away His authority from them when the enemy of Allah, Iblis, said: ﴿And I will surely mislead them all, ﴿except among them Your chosen servants﴾﴾ [al-Hijr: 39–40], and Allah the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators﴾ [al-Hijr: 42]. Regarding the meaning of "authority" there are two views. One: proof (hujjah), and from it the ruler is called "sultan" because he is the proof of Allah the Most High on earth.

The second: that it is power (qudrah), derived from "al-sultah," and likewise the sovereign is called "sultan" for his power.

﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾, meaning: who follow him.

﴿And those who are, through him, polytheists﴾. Regarding this there are three sayings. The first: "And those who are, through Allah, polytheists." This was said by Mujahid.

The second: "And those who associated Satan in their deeds." This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The third: "And those who, for the sake of Satan and obedience to him, are polytheists." This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another﴾ — concerning this there are two interpretations.

One: it is a law (shari'ah) that preceded, replaced by a new law. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The second, and it is the view of the majority (jumhur): that is, We abrogated one verse with another, either by abrogating the ruling and the recitation together, or by abrogating the ruling while the recitation remains.

﴿And Allah knows best what He sends down﴾ — meaning, He knows best the benefit in it: He sends it down as abrogating (nasikh) and lifts it up as abrogated (mansukh) (naskh is the term for abrogation).

﴿But most of them do not know﴾ — concerning this there are two interpretations. One: they do not know that abrogation (naskh) is permissible. The second: they do not know the reason for the occurrence of abrogation.

The second, and it is the view of the majority (jumhur): that is, We abrogated one verse with another, either by abrogating the ruling and the recitation together, or by abrogating the ruling while the recitation remains.

﴿And Allah knows best what He sends down﴾ — meaning, He knows best the benefit in it: He sends it down as abrogating (nasikh) and lifts it up as abrogated (mansukh) (naskh is the term for abrogation).

﴿They say, "You are only a fabricator"﴾ — that is, a liar.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾ — concerning this there are two interpretations. One: they do not know that abrogation (naskh) is permissible. The second: they do not know the reason for the occurrence of abrogation.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verses 103–105:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We certainly know that they say, "It is only a human being who teaches him."﴾ The scholars differed about the identity of the person whom the polytheists meant by their claim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was being taught, and they gave four opinions.

The first: he was Bal'am (Bal'am), a blacksmith (qayn) in Mecca. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to enter upon him and he would teach him, so the Quraysh accused him of learning from him. This is related from Mujahid.

The second: he was a non-Arab (a'jami) slave belonging to a woman in Mecca, called Abu Fukayha. He used to visit the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, reciting to him and learning from him. So they said to his mistress, "Confine him," and she confined him. She also said to him, "Sweep the house and eat its refuse," and he did so, and he said, "By Allah, I have never eaten anything better or sweeter than it." After that he would ask his mistress to confine him, but she would not do so.

The third: they were two boys belonging to Banu al-Hadrami, who were from the people of 'Ayn al-Tamr, polishers (sayqalan) who worked on swords. The name of one of them was Yasar and the other was Jabr. They used to read the Torah, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would sometimes sit with them. This is said by Husayn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim.

The fourth: he was Salman al-Farisi. This is said by al-Dahhak.

﴿The tongue of the one they refer to is foreign,﴾ Regarding "yulhidun" (they refer/incline) there are two interpretations. One: they incline towards him. The second: they raise objections through it, meaning that the tongue of the one whom they attributed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as his teacher is foreign.

﴿And this is a clear Arabic tongue.﴾ By "the tongue" is meant the Qur'an, because it is recited with the tongue. The Arabs say, "This is the tongue of so-and-so," meaning his speech. The poet said:

"The evil tongue you bring to us, and you betrayed, and I did not think you would betray us."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verses 106–109:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his faith﴾. Al-Kalbi mentioned that it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, Miqyas ibn Subabah, ʿAbd Allah ibn Khatal and Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, who disbelieved after their faith.

Then He said, the Exalted: ﴿Except one who has been compelled while his heart is at rest with faith﴾. Al-Kalbi said: This was revealed concerning ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, his parents Yasir and Sumayyah, Bilal, Suhayb and Khabbab, who manifested disbelief under compulsion while their hearts were at rest with faith.

Then He said, the Exalted: ﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾, and they are those mentioned earlier. So when one is compelled to disbelief and he utters it with his tongue while he holds faith in his heart, in order to ward off from himself by what he manifested and to preserve his religion by what he concealed, he remains upon his faith; but if he did not conceal it, he would be a disbeliever.

Some of the theologians said: It is only permissible for the one under compulsion to express disbelief by way of allusion (taʿrid) rather than by an outright, explicit statement (tasrih batt).

This is because of the ugliness and gravity of explicitly declaring someone a liar, both in custom and in the Shariʿah, such as saying: "Muhammad is a liar in your belief," or pointing to another person whose name matches his name when it is known that he is a liar. "By my life, this is the better of the two matters." And the one compelled does not become a disbeliever by explicit statement.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verses 110–113:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah presents an example: a town that was secure and tranquil﴾. By "the town" He means its people. ﴿Secure﴾, meaning free from fear.

﴿Tranquil﴾, with abundance and ease.

﴿Its provision came to it﴾. Regarding this there are two views. One: its sustenance (aqwat). The second: what it desired (muraduha).

﴿Plentifully﴾. Regarding this there are two views. One: good (tayyiban). The second: wholesome, without hardship (hani'an).

﴿From every place﴾, meaning from it through agriculture and from elsewhere through trade, so that the combination of the two would be more abundant for their settlement and more general in the blessing upon them.

﴿But it denied the favours of Allah﴾. This may bear two meanings. One: by abandoning His thanks and obedience. The second: by not giving its due of sharing with the poor and aiding those in need.

Regarding this town which Allah, may He be exalted, presented as an example, there are several opinions. The first: that it is Makkah, whose security was that its people were secure and were not snatched away as the people of the desert were.

﴿So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear﴾. He called it a garment because the hunger and fear may appear upon them in the form of emaciation, paleness of complexion and bad condition, which is like a garment. It was said that the famine reached them to the point that they ate the qadd (dried leather) and the 'ilhiz, which is wool mixed with blood. The qadd is a hide that is eaten. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: that it is Madinah, which believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then denied the favours of Allah by the killing of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and by the trials that occurred there after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the view of 'A'ishah and Hafsah, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The third: that it is a parable struck for any town that was in this description among the other towns.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 114–119:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Then indeed your Lord — for those who did evil in ignorance﴾. In it there are two interpretations. The first: "in ignorance" meaning in ignorance that it is evil.

The second: "in ignorance" due to the dominance of desire over them, together with knowledge that it is evil.

And it may admit a third: that it is the one who hastens to commit it and promises himself repentance.

﴿Then they repent after that and make amends﴾. Because mere repentance from what has passed, if one does not amend his conduct in what follows, does not deserve nor merit reward.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verses 120–123:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation﴾. There are three interpretations concerning it. The first: he was one who knows good (ʿālim al-khayr). This was said by Ibn Masʿūd and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī.

Zuhayr said:

"Peoples honored him, from every noble company; and if you deny me, ask the nations."

He means: the scholars.

The second: he was a nation that is followed (yuqtadā bihi). This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. He was called a nation because the nation stood by him.

The third: he was an imam who is followed (yu'tamm bihi). This was said by al-Kisāʾī and Abū ʿUbayda.

﴿Devoutly obedient to Allah﴾. There are three interpretations concerning it. (p-219) The first: obedient to Allah. This was said by Ibn Masʿūd.

The second: the qānit is the one who persists in worship of Allah.

The third: one who supplicates to Allah, exalted is He, much.

﴿Ḥanīfan﴾ (upright). There are three interpretations concerning it. The first: sincere (mukhliṣ). This was said by Muqātil.

The second: a pilgrim (ḥājj). This was said by al-Kalbī.

The third: that he was one who stays upon the path of truth. This was related by Ibn ʿĪsā.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾. Concerning it there are two aspects. The first: he was not of those who associate partners by worshipping idols.

The second: he did not see withholding and giving except from Allah.

﴿And We gave him in this world a good [reward]﴾. Concerning it there are four interpretations. The first: the good [reward] is prophethood. This was said by al-Ḥasan.

The second: a tongue of truthfulness (lisān ṣidq). This was said by Mujāhid.

The third: that all the people of the religions take him as their ally and are pleased with him. This was said by Qatāda.

The fourth: that it is Allah's exalting his mention in this world by his obedience to his Lord. This was related by Ibn ʿĪsā.

And it may admit a fifth: that it is the continuance of his hospitality and the visits of the nations to his grave.

﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter, he is among the righteous﴾. Concerning it there are two aspects. The first: in the dwellings of the righteous in Paradise.

The second: among the messengers brought near.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, ḥanīfan﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions. The first: following him in all of his religion except what he was commanded to abandon. This is the saying of some companions of al-Shāfiʿī, and this is evidence for the permissibility of the superior following the inferior, because the Prophet ﷺ is the best of the prophets.

The second: following him in disavowing idols and adhering to Islam. This was said by Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭabarī.(p-220)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verses 120–123:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation﴾. There are three interpretations concerning it. The first: he was one who knows good (ʿālim al-khayr). This was said by Ibn Masʿūd and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī.

Zuhayr said:

"Peoples honored him, from every noble company; and if you deny me, ask the nations."

He means: the scholars.

The second: he was a nation that is followed (yuqtadā bihi). This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. He was called a nation because the nation stood by him.

The third: he was an imam who is followed (yu'tamm bihi). This was said by al-Kisāʾī and Abū ʿUbayda.

﴿Devoutly obedient to Allah﴾. There are three interpretations concerning it. (p-219) The first: obedient to Allah. This was said by Ibn Masʿūd.

The second: the qānit is the one who persists in worship of Allah.

The third: one who supplicates to Allah, exalted is He, much.

﴿Ḥanīfan﴾ (upright). There are three interpretations concerning it. The first: sincere (mukhliṣ). This was said by Muqātil.

The second: a pilgrim (ḥājj). This was said by al-Kalbī.

The third: that he was one who stays upon the path of truth. This was related by Ibn ʿĪsā.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾. Concerning it there are two aspects. The first: he was not of those who associate partners by worshipping idols.

The second: he did not see withholding and giving except from Allah.

﴿And We gave him in this world a good [reward]﴾. Concerning it there are four interpretations. The first: the good [reward] is prophethood. This was said by al-Ḥasan.

The second: a tongue of truthfulness (lisān ṣidq). This was said by Mujāhid.

The third: that all the people of the religions take him as their ally and are pleased with him. This was said by Qatāda.

The fourth: that it is Allah's exalting his mention in this world by his obedience to his Lord. This was related by Ibn ʿĪsā.

And it may admit a fifth: that it is the continuance of his hospitality and the visits of the nations to his grave.

﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter, he is among the righteous﴾. Concerning it there are two aspects. The first: in the dwellings of the righteous in Paradise.

The second: among the messengers brought near.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 124:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it﴾. They are the Jews. Regarding their disagreement about the Sabbath, there are three opinions:

First: some of them made it the greatest of days in sanctity, because Allah finished creating things on it.

Second: some of them made Sunday greater in sanctity than it, because Allah began the creation of things on it.

Third: they deviated from what they were commanded concerning the glorification of Friday, giving precedence to the sanctity of Saturday and Sunday. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verse 125:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord﴾ means: to the religion of your Lord, which is Islam.

﴿With wisdom﴾ — concerning it there are two interpretations. One of them: with the Qur'an; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: with prophethood; this is a possibility.

﴿And good admonition﴾ — concerning it there are two interpretations. One of them: with the Qur'an, in gentle speech; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: with what it contains of commands and prohibitions; this was said by Muqatil.

﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ — concerning it there are four aspects. The first: meaning, with forgiveness.

The second: by awakening the hearts and not belittling the intellects.

The third: by guiding the later generation and not blaming the earlier generation.

The fourth: according to what they can bear.

Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "We, the company of prophets, have been commanded to speak to people according to the level of their intellects."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 16, verses 126–128:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions. The first: it was revealed concerning the martyrs of Uhud, when the Quraysh mutilated them.

Those who hold this view differ over whether it was abrogated (naskh) into two positions. The first: it is abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not but through Allah﴾. The second: it is established and not abrogated. This is one of the two opinions.

The second opinion: it was revealed concerning every wronged person who may seek retribution from his wrongdoer. This was said by Ibn Sirin and Mujahid. ﴿And be patient﴾ has two meanings. The first: be patient over the harm that has befallen you, and this is a possibility.

The second: be patient by forgoing punishing them with the like of what they did, namely the mutilation of the martyrs of Uhud. This was said by al-Kalbi.

﴿And your patience is not but through Allah﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: your patience is not but by the help of Allah.

(p-222) The second: your patience is not but for the sake of Allah.

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾ has two meanings. The first: if they do not accept. The second: if they do not believe.

﴿And do not be in distress over what they plot﴾. Ibn Kathir read ﴿ḍayqin﴾ with a kasra, and the rest read it with a fatha.

Regarding the distinction between the two, there are two opinions. The first: with the fatha is what is little, and with the kasra is what is much; this was said by Abu 'Ubayda. The second: with the fatha is what is in the chest, and with the kasra is what is in a place that widens and narrows; this was said by al-Farra'.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who are mindful of Him and those who are doers of good﴾. "Those who are mindful of Him" means in regard to what Allah has forbidden for them.

"Those who are doers of good" means in regard to what Allah has enjoined. Thus this verse combines avoiding sins and performing acts of obedience.

His saying: ﴿with those who are mindful of Him﴾ means: the helper of those who are mindful of Allah.

Some of the people of insight said: whoever is mindful of Allah in his actions, Allah will be good to him in his circumstances. And Allah knows best.
